1.title: IPv4 Addressing and Subnetting
1.text: Welcome to Module six: IPv four Addressing and Subnetting. It covers the exam area one point zero Networking Concepts. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. one point seven Given a scenario, use appropriate IPv four network addressing: public versus private (A P I P A, R F C nineteen eighteen, loopback). Subnetting (V L S M, C I D R). IPv four address classes A to E. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: one point zero Networking Concepts (twenty-three percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred twenty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Network plus N ten to nine exam objectives, version four point zero.

1.title: IPv4 basics
1.text: IPv four basics. An IPv four address is thirty-two bits, written as four decimal numbers (octets), for example one hundred ninety-two dot one hundred sixty-eight dot ten dot twenty-five. It has a network part and a host part, split by the subnet mask ( two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot zero ) or the C I D R prefix ( slash twenty-four ).

1.title: IPv4 basics, continued
1.text: IPv four basics. Class A. First octet: one to one hundred twenty-six. Default mask: two hundred fifty-five dot zero dot zero dot zero ( slash eight). Use: Very large networks. Class B. First octet: one hundred twenty-eight to one hundred ninety-one. Default mask: two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot zero dot zero ( slash sixteen). Use: Medium networks. Class C. First octet: one hundred ninety-two to two hundred twenty-three. Default mask: two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot zero ( slash twenty-four). Use: Small networks. Class D. First octet: two hundred twenty-four to two hundred thirty-nine. Default mask: not applicable. Use: Multicast. Class E. First octet: two hundred forty to two hundred fifty-five. Default mask: not applicable. Use: Reserved, experimental. one hundred twenty-seven dot zero dot zero dot zero slash eight is loopback (class A space, not used for networks).

1.title: Public, private and special addresses
1.text: Public, private and special addresses. R F C nineteen eighteen private. ten dot zero dot zero dot zero slash eight, one hundred seventy-two dot sixteen dot zero dot zero slash twelve (one hundred seventy-two dot sixteen dot zero dot zero to one hundred seventy-two dot thirty-one dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five), one hundred ninety-two dot one hundred sixty-eight dot zero dot zero slash sixteen; not routed on the internet, need nat. Public. Everything else routable on the internet. A P I P A (Automatic Private I P Addressing). one hundred sixty-nine dot two hundred fifty-four dot zero dot zero slash sixteen; a host assigns itself this address when D H C P fails. Loopback. one hundred twenty-seven dot zero dot zero dot one (localhost): tests the local T C P or I P stack. Exam tip: A host with one sixty-nine dot two fifty-four dot x dot x cannot reach the D H C P server. one hundred twenty-seven dot zero dot zero dot one tests the host's own stack.

1.title: Subnetting
1.text: Subnetting. The figure shows this: Subnetting: borrowing host bits, block size and the network, broadcast and usable range.

1.title: Subnetting, continued
1.text: Subnetting. C I D R (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) writes the mask as a prefix length and ignores the old classes. V L S M (variable length subnet mask) lets different subnets use different prefix lengths to fit each segment without wasting addresses. slash twenty-four. Mask: two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot zero. Addresses: two hundred fifty-six. Usable hosts: two hundred fifty-four. slash twenty-five. Mask: two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot one hundred twenty-eight. Addresses: one hundred twenty-eight. Usable hosts: one hundred twenty-six. slash twenty-six. Mask: two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot one hundred ninety-two. Addresses: sixty-four. Usable hosts: sixty-two. slash twenty-seven. Mask: two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred twenty-four. Addresses: thirty-two. Usable hosts: thirty. slash twenty-eight. Mask: two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred forty. Addresses: sixteen. Usable hosts: fourteen. slash twenty-nine. Mask: two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred forty-eight. Addresses: eight. Usable hosts: six. slash thirty. Mask: two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-two. Addresses: four. Usable hosts: two. Formulas: addresses equals two^(thirty-two − prefix); usable hosts equals addresses − two (network and broadcast); number of subnets equals two^(borrowed bits).

1.title: A worked example
1.text: A worked example. Network one hundred ninety-two dot one hundred sixty-eight dot ten dot zero slash twenty-four split into slash twenty-six subnets: block size sixty-four, subnets start at.zero,.sixty-four,.one hundred twenty-eight,.one hundred ninety-two. For one hundred ninety-two dot one hundred sixty-eight dot ten dot seventy slash twenty-six: network one hundred ninety-two dot one hundred sixty-eight dot ten dot sixty-four, broadcast one hundred ninety-two dot one hundred sixty-eight dot ten dot one hundred twenty-seven, usable.sixty-five to.one hundred twenty-six (sixty-two hosts). Exam tip: Block size equals two hundred fifty-six − the interesting octet of the mask. For two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five dot one hundred ninety-two, block size equals sixty-four. The first address of a block is the network; the last is the broadcast; the rest are hosts. Exam tip: Usable hosts equals two to the power of the host bits, minus two. A slash thirty has two hosts, a slash twenty-nine has six, a slash twenty-eight has fourteen.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. How many usable host addresses does a slash twenty-six subnet provide? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: sixty-two. A slash twenty-six has sixty-four addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. What is the broadcast address of one hundred ninety-two dot one hundred sixty-eight dot ten dot seventy slash twenty-six? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: one hundred ninety-two dot one hundred sixty-eight dot ten dot one hundred twenty-seven. The block runs from.sixty-four to.one hundred twenty-seven, so.one hundred twenty-seven is the broadcast address.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A workstation shows the address one hundred sixty-nine dot two hundred fifty-four dot twelve dot eight after boot. What does this indicate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: It could not obtain an address from a D H C P server. Self-assigned A P I P A addresses appear when D H C P fails.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which address is a private R F C nineteen eighteen address? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: one hundred seventy-two dot twenty dot five dot nine. one hundred seventy-two dot sixteen dot zero dot zero to one hundred seventy-two dot thirty-one dot two hundred fifty-five dot two hundred fifty-five is private; one hundred seventy-two point three two and one hundred ninety-two point one six nine are public.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. An engineer needs a subnet for twenty-eight hosts and wants the smallest suitable prefix. Which should be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: slash twenty-seven. A slash twenty-seven provides thirty usable hosts; slash twenty-eight provides only fourteen.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which technique lets different subnets in one network use different mask lengths? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Variable length subnet masking. V L S M fits each subnet to its size.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. How many bits is an IPv four address? Answer: thirty-two. Question two. What is the formula for usable hosts? Answer: two to the power of the host bits, minus two. Question three. What is the loopback address? Answer: one hundred twenty-seven dot zero dot zero dot one.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What range does A P I P A use? Answer: one hundred sixty-nine dot two hundred fifty-four dot zero dot zero slash sixteen. Question five. What is the class of an address starting at one hundred fifty? Answer: Class B. Question six. What does C I D R replace? Answer: The fixed address classes.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Classes: A one to one hundred twenty-six, B one hundred twenty-eight to one hundred ninety-one, C one hundred ninety-two to two hundred twenty-three, D multicast, E reserved. Private: ten or eight, one hundred seventy-two point one six or twelve, one hundred ninety-two point one six eight or sixteen; A P I P A one hundred sixty-nine point two five four or sixteen. Math: addresses two^(thirty-two-prefix); hosts minus two; block size two hundred fifty-six - mask octet. Common prefixes: slash twenty-four two hundred fifty-four, slash twenty-five one hundred twenty-six, slash twenty-six sixty-two, slash twenty-seven thirty, slash twenty-eight fourteen, slash twenty-nine six, slash thirty two.
